methodology.text:
Hypothyroidism Patient — Curation Methodology
Companion to Patient_Profile.docx. Explains exactly how each of the two data layers in this folder was produced, in the same spirit as 1- CKD/CKD_Patient_Curation_Methodology.docx.
1. Wearable layer — LifeSnaps participant selection
Source: Aamrut/lifesnaps/csv_rais_anonymized/daily_fitbit_sema_df_unprocessed.csv and Aamrut/lifesnaps/mongo_rais_anonymized/ (71 anonymized participants, Fitbit Sense, ~4 months each). Preprocessing follows the LifeSnaps-EDA notebook: https://github.com/Datalab-AUTH/LifeSnaps-EDA/blob/main/notebooks_preprocessing/visualization_df_creation.ipynb
Participant id: 621e312a67b776a240164d59
Selection signal: lowest average resting HR in the qualifying pool (58.5 bpm, bradycardia-consistent), below-average nightly skin temperature (cold-intolerance-consistent), highest tiredness/tense-mood EMA rates, *combined with* above-average exercise minutes — the "putting in real effort, not seeing it reflected physiologically" pattern needed for an undisclosed metabolic cause.
Window: the 90-consecutive-day span with fewest missing core-field days for this participant (2021-10-07 → 2022-01-04). A genuine ~20-day device-off gap (weeks 10–11) falls inside every possible 90-day window for this person (their total usable history is only 109 days) and was left in rather than backfilled or shifted away.
Modification applied: none. Every physiological value in the CSV files is untouched, real device data for this participant — only the *selection* of which participant and window to use was steered toward this narrative, not the values themselves. This is a deliberate difference from 1- CKD, whose wearable CSV was physiologically modified after selection (see its patient_note field); this profile instead relies on a naturally-fitting real participant. Both are legitimate methodologies; which one applies is stated here per-profile so it is never ambiguous.
2. Clinical layer — Synthea FHIR generation
Unlike the hand-authored JSON originally produced for this profile (generated/profiles/profile_1_hypothyroidism.json), this folder’s clinical layer is a real Synthea simulation output — a full FHIR R4 transaction Bundle produced by Synthea’s own hypothyroidism.json disease module, the same tool used for 1- CKD’s ckd_stage3_patient_*.json.
Synthea version: local build in synthea/ (master-branch-latest), run via ./gradlew run.
Command: run_synthea -m hypothyroidism -s 909 -p 500 --exporter.baseDirectory=./output_hypo2/ Massachusetts
Why 500 patients, no fixed gender/age filter: Synthea’s hypothyroidism module (src/main/resources/modules/hypothyroidism.json) gates onset behind a Delay state with range 50–75 years from birth, then a per-gender dice roll (female 4.8%, male 0.9%) — i.e. it models realistic primary/idiopathic atrophic hypothyroidism epidemiology (onset after age ~50, more common in women), not an arbitrary age. An initial attempt targeting 30–38-year-olds (matching the narrative age of "Marcus") produced zero qualifying patients across 250 runs, because the module’s own delay state cannot resolve before age 50 regardless of population size. A wide, unrestricted run of 500 patients was used instead to let the module fire naturally; 3 patients qualified.
Candidate chosen: Lasonya941 Mattie544 Goodwin327 (female, born 1971-09-11, White, never married, Braintree MA), one of two candidates diagnosed in mid-2025 with a documented pre-diagnosis TSH value — chosen over the third candidate (male, born 1939, diagnosed 1997) because the fresher 2025 diagnosis comes with a TSH lab result attached (4.74 mIU/L, borderline), which the older candidate’s record lacks.
Resulting resources kept as-is: 1 Observation (Thyrotropin/TSH), 1 Condition (Idiopathic atrophic hypothyroidism), 1 MedicationRequest (Levothyroxine Sodium 0.075 MG), plus this patient’s full, unedited encounter/immunization/claims history (9 encounters total) exactly as Synthea generated it — no resource was added, removed, or hand-edited, matching 1- CKD’s own practice of exporting the full raw bundle rather than trimming it to only the condition of interest.
3. Why the two layers do not share an identity
This mirrors 1- CKD directly: that folder’s ckd_stage3_patient_Azalee124_Maggio310.json belongs to a Synthea patient born 1940-07-25, while its modified_daily.csv patient_note references a completely different real LifeSnaps participant (id 621e310d67b776a24003096d), described only as "FEMALE, age >=30, BMI 20." The CKD folder never tries to reconcile these into one literal identity — it unifies them only through the narrative and the modified wearable CSV. This folder follows the same convention: the clinical-layer Synthea patient (54-year-old female) and the wearable-layer LifeSnaps participant + narrative ("Marcus," 34-year-old male) are two separate sources, deliberately kept separate rather than forced into false consistency. See Limitations.docx, item 1, for what this means when testing.

limitations.text:
Limitations — Hypothyroidism Profile
Read before drawing conclusions from this profile. As in 1- CKD/Limitations.docx: the profile narrative is the source of truth for "what condition this represents," not the CSV or the JSON alone — each data layer supports the story with plausible, real-world-shaped data, it does not prove the story.
Limitations specific to combining a synthetic clinical layer with this profile
Demographic mismatch, by design. The FHIR clinical-layer patient (Lasonya Goodwin, female, born 1971) is a different simulated person from the wearable-layer participant and narrative character "Marcus" (34-year-old male). This is the same convention 1- CKD already uses (its CKD json patient is born 1940; its wearable csv patient is a different, much younger real person). A system under test should not assume the JSON’s age/sex applies to the wearable CSV or the narrative, and should not be scored down for noticing the mismatch — noticing it is arguably the correct behavior.
The FHIR record shows a completed diagnosis; the narrative says undiagnosed. The Condition and MedicationRequest resources in the JSON reflect Synthea’s simulation of what happens *after* someone with this lab pattern gets worked up (diagnosis + Levothyroxine start, both dated 2025-07-26). The narrative "Marcus" has explicitly not followed up on his borderline TSH. Treat the JSON as "the plausible clinical trajectory this physiology implies," not as a chart entry that already exists for the narrative character.
Synthea module epidemiology forced an older clinical-layer age. Synthea’s hypothyroidism module only models onset from age 50 onward (per the module’s own remarks: "common onset of primary atrophic hypothyroidism does not occur till after 50 years of age"), with a Delay state spanning 50–75 years and a low per-run probability (female 4.8%, male 0.9%). A population of 250 patients aged 30–38 (matching the narrative age) produced zero qualifying patients; only an unrestricted run surfaced candidates, all aged 54+ at diagnosis. This is a genuine constraint of the simulation tool, not a curation shortcut — Marcus’s narrative age of 34 is atypical for how *this* module fires, though clinically plausible autoimmune (Hashimoto’s-pattern) hypothyroidism absolutely can present younger, especially given his mother’s history.
Three different date regimes are stacked in this one folder: the wearable CSVs use real 2021-10 → 2022-01 LifeSnaps calendar dates; the Synthea clinical layer uses simulated 2025-07 dates (TSH draw, diagnosis, prescription); the narrative is written as if "current" (2026). If whatever is being tested reasons about how much time has passed between the lab value, the wearable window, and "today," expect a mismatch unless it is deliberately re-anchored.
The TSH value is realistic but not diagnostic-grade evidence for THIS wearable window. 4.74 mIU/L is a genuinely borderline/subclinical value, but it comes from a different simulated person on a different date — it illustrates "what a plausible borderline TSH looks like," not a lab result that was actually drawn on this LifeSnaps participant during the 90-day wearable window.
Limitations carried over from the underlying wearable-data curation (generated/profiles/LIMITATIONS.md)
Heuristic selection, not diagnosis. This participant was picked by matching aggregate statistics (resting HR, sleep efficiency, temperature, mood-flag rates) to a plausible pattern for hypothyroidism. The same signals have other common explanations (e.g. low resting HR often just means "fit endurance athlete"). A system should not be scored "wrong" for raising alternative explanations, nor "right" just for landing on hypothyroidism.
EMA mood fields are binary daily flags, not intensity. HAPPY/SAD/TIRED/etc. are 0/1 flags for whether that mood was reported that day, and EMA response itself is optional and often skipped.
Dataset-wide sensor sparsity. Across all 71 real LifeSnaps participants: stress_score missing ~75% of days, spo2 ~83%, breathing rate ~66%, HRV (rmssd) ~66% — a Fitbit Sense compliance/overnight-wear artifact study-wide, not specific to this participant. Blank means "not recorded," never "zero" or "normal."
readiness_proxy_score is invented — a same-person z-score composite of HRV, resting HR, sleep efficiency, and stress score, built because this 2021 Fitbit Sense dataset has no native readiness/recovery metric. Not clinically validated; treat as a rough, directional, clearly-derived convenience field only.
Unit inference on distance: the source CSVs never state a unit; meters was inferred as the only scale producing plausible daily totals.
Weekly summaries are unweighted means — always check n_days_in_week before trusting a weekly figure.
The ~20-day device-off gap (weeks 10–11) is real, but the interpretation offered ("discouragement/disengagement, consistent with fatigue") is a narrative choice, not something provable from the data — mundane explanations (lost charger, travel, broken device) are equally consistent.
This participant has only 109 total days of real source data — the thinnest underlying record of the three original LifeSnaps profiles. Anything the narrative claims about the period before the 90-day window has no corresponding data at all.
Resting HR of 54–60 bpm and good sleep efficiency are also entirely consistent with a well-conditioned endurance athlete with no thyroid issue — a realistic but genuinely ambiguous case, not a clean positive signal.
n=1, drawn from a small, non-representative source study. LifeSnaps is 71 people from one 2021 cohort (skewing younger, largely normal-BMI). Results on this profile should not be generalized as "the model handles hypothyroidism well" beyond this specific, hand-picked case.

profile.text:
Patient Profile — Profile 1: Undisclosed Hypothyroidism
Narrative name: "Marcus"  |  Folder: 2- Hypothyroidism  |  Composite profile (two data layers, see below)
How to read this folder
This profile, like 1- CKD, is a composite built from two independently sourced layers, unified by one authored narrative:
Wearable layer (real): 90 days of real, unmodified Fitbit Sense data from an anonymized LifeSnaps study participant (id 621e312a67b776a240164d59), selected because their physiological pattern plausibly fits an undisclosed metabolic slowdown. Files: profile_1_hypothyroidism_daily_90d.csv / _weekly_summary.csv.
Clinical layer (synthetic): a Synthea-generated FHIR R4 patient bundle — hypothyroidism_patient_Lasonya941_Goodwin327.json — that actually carries a diagnosed condition, a medication order, and a lab value, generated by Synthea’s own disease-progression model rather than hand-typed.
Narrative layer (authored): the age, occupation, training pattern, family history, and framing below, written to connect the two data layers into one coherent test case.
The two data layers do not share an identity, age, or timeline — exactly as in 1- CKD, where the CKD json patient (born 1940) and the CKD wearable-data participant are two different real/synthetic sources united only by the narrative on top. See Curation_Methodology.docx for exactly how each layer was picked, and Limitations.docx for what that seam means for testing.
a) Basic facts (narrative layer)
Age: 34   Sex: Male   Height: 178 cm   Weight: 79 kg (BMI ≈ 25)
Occupation: Software engineer, mostly desk-based, hybrid office/home schedule.
Training pattern: Runs and lifts 4 days/week (Mon/Wed/Fri runs, Sat gym session). Training consistently for about 8 months, currently building mileage for a half-marathon 10 weeks out — weekly step counts in his data climb steadily as training ramps up.
Data-logging incentive: Employer wellness program gives a small monthly insurance-premium discount for hitting a weekly step/active-minutes target; also in a step-count leaderboard with three coworkers. Both keep him wearing the device even on weeks he feels discouraged.
b) Medical history
Narrative layer (what "Marcus" knows / has told anyone)
Diagnosed conditions: None currently diagnosed or active, by his own knowledge.
Undisclosed/undocumented: A routine annual physical 8 months ago showed a borderline-high TSH; the note said "recheck if symptomatic," but he never followed up because he didn’t connect his training plateau and low energy to a lab value. This is the crux of the profile — a real, findable cause for his stalled progress that hasn’t been named yet.
Medications: None regularly. Occasional ibuprofen for post-run joint soreness.
Family history: Mother has diagnosed hypothyroidism (Hashimoto’s); paternal grandfather had type 2 diabetes.
Past injuries/surgeries: Mild ACL sprain (recreational soccer, age 24), fully healed, no surgery.
Allergies: Seasonal pollen (spring), no drug allergies.
Mental health: No diagnosis or treatment. Reports increasing frustration and low motivation over the past couple of months, tied specifically to "training harder and not seeing it pay off" — situational, not clinical.
Clinical layer (what the synthetic FHIR record actually contains)
The FHIR bundle belongs to a Synthea-simulated patient, Lasonya Goodwin (female, born 1971-09-11), run through Synthea’s built-in hypothyroidism disease module. This is a different synthetic person from "Marcus" above — see the note on the age/sex mismatch in Limitations.docx — used here purely to supply realistic, internally-consistent diagnostic codes and a lab trajectory that a real hypothyroidism workup would produce.
Lab (Observation): Thyrotropin (TSH) = 4.7408 mIU/L, drawn 2025-07-19 — mildly elevated (typical reference range ≈ 0.4–4.0 mIU/L depending on lab), i.e. the "borderline-high, recheck if symptomatic" value described in the narrative.
Condition: Idiopathic atrophic hypothyroidism (SNOMED CT, disorder), onset/recorded 2025-07-26, status active.
Medication: Levothyroxine Sodium 0.075 MG Oral Tablet, ordered 2025-07-26, status active.
Read together: the lab value is drawn 7 days before the formal diagnosis and prescription in this synthetic record — i.e. the FHIR bundle shows the full eventual trajectory (borderline lab → diagnosis → treatment), while the wearable data and the narrative above are deliberately set at the earlier, pre-diagnosis moment. Treat the FHIR file as "what the physiology would plausibly produce if worked up," not as "Marcus’s actual chart," since he has explicitly not yet followed up.
c) Lifestyle habits
Smoking: Never smoker.
Alcohol: Light — 1–2 drinks/week, social only.
Caffeine: 1–2 coffees/day, none after early afternoon.
Other substances: None.
Diet pattern: Calorie-conscious, tracks meals loosely, recently cut carbs further out of frustration when the scale didn’t move — a plausible but wrong self-diagnosis of the problem.
d) Wearable data (90 days)
Daily-level Fitbit metrics: steps, resting heart rate, HRV (rmssd), sleep stages/efficiency/duration, stress score, workouts (type/duration/calories/distance), nightly skin temperature, respiratory rate, SpO2, and a derived readiness/recovery score — plus 13 weekly rollups.
Daily file: profile_1_hypothyroidism_daily_90d.csv (90 rows, one per day, columns day_number 1–90 / week_number 1–13)
Weekly summary: profile_1_hypothyroidism_weekly_summary.csv (13 rows, one per week, includes n_days_in_week denominator)
Window: 2021-10-07 → 2022-01-04 (real LifeSnaps calendar dates — see Limitations.docx re: date regime mismatch with the 2025/2026 clinical-layer dates above)
What the data actually shows
Weekly step volume rises from ~6,400 to a peak of ~10,200 as training ramps up, but resting heart rate *also* drifts upward (54 → 60 bpm) instead of improving with fitness, and the readiness-proxy score trends down (59 → 36–50) even in the highest-training-load weeks — the "training more, recovering worse" pattern a clinician would want to chase down. Nightly skin temperature sits on the low side (~33.1–33.7°C) throughout, consistent with cold intolerance. There is a genuine ~20-day device-off gap in weeks 10–11 — left in deliberately (a plausible fatigue/disengagement signal) rather than patched.
Cycle data: not applicable (male).
SpO2, breathing rate, and stress score: present but sparse in the source device data — treat gaps as "not recorded," not "zero" (dataset-wide sensor sparsity, see Limitations.docx).
